newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO shows force in Mostar to prevent escalation.
newsitem.headline: NATO shows force in Mostar to prevent escalation.

text.p: NATO troops deployed to prevent an escalation of violence in the ethnically divided Bosnian town of Mostar on Tuesday after at least one person was killed and 22 were wounded.

Western powers called on the Zagreb government to rein in their ethnic kin in Bosnia after local Croats, including policemen, opened fire on a Moslem crowd visiting a cemetery in the Croat part of town on Monday.

Shortly after the shooting, the worst violence in the southern town since the war ended in 1995, Bosnian Croats evicted some 26 Moslems from their homes, mainly from an apartment building opposite the main Croat police station.

In a show of force, NATO-led SFOR troops deployed in large numbers with armoured vehicles at key intersections on both sides of the former Mostar frontline, stopping cars at random and searching them for illegal weapons.
A Reuters reporter witnessed French troops finding an automatic rifle with several magazines of ammunition, two grenades and a pistol in one car. The weapons were confiscated.

Senior Moslem and Croat police officials, meeting at the Mostar airport on Tuesday, agreed to enforce a strict curfew from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., and to reinforce local police patrols with international policemen.

Despite the increased NATO presence, tension remained high, but Western observers say there is little chance that the stand-off will escalate into a full-scale battle as neither side enjoys a clear military advantage over other.
While NATO was sorting things out on the ground, Bosnian Croats and their backers in Croatia came under a barrage of protests from Western governments and international peace envoys.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel urged Zagreb to exert control over Bosnia's Croats and prevent a recurrence of attacks on Moslems in Mostar.

Kinkel said he had instructed Bonn's ambassador in Zagreb to visit the Croatian government "so that it lives up to its responsibilities in the Dayton Agreement and exerts its influence on those with responsibility in Mostar".
The United States, whose diplomacy ended a Moslem-Croat war in 1994 and set up a shaky bi-national Federation, condemned the violence and implicitly blamed the Croats.

"We are calling upon the Croatian authorities and the Croatian civilians involved to exercise maximum restraint and not to repeat this kind of aggressive activity," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

U.N. human rights envoy Elisabeth Rehn called on Bosnian Croats to remove from power those responsible for creating tensions and widening ethnic divides "including elements of electronic and printed media".

"I am also aware that the authorities of the Republic of Croatia are exercising serious influence in the region and therefore also bear responsibility for the human rights prevailing there," Rehn said in a letter to Kresimir Zubak, Croat president of the Moslem-Croat Bosnian Federation.
Zagreb is seen as standing behind hard-line Bosnian Croats who seek a separate state in the part of southwestern Bosnia under their control.
Croatian President Franjo Tudjman called his Bosnian counterpart Alija Izetbegovic to discuss the situation in Mostar, the Croatian state news agency Hina said.

The two presidents agreed that an independent commission should investigate causes and responsibility for the incident and the culprits be held responsible, Hina said, quoting a statement from Tudjman's office.
Croatian television, quoting witnesses, said two Croats were killed near Mostar on the highway linking the capital Sarajevo with the Adriatic port of Ploce.
It said three Croat policemen were stabbed with knives during the Monday incident while 26 civilians were injured, mostly by Moslem policemen and civilians on the Sarajevo road.
Independent sources could not verify reports of Croats injured on Monday, nor of fatalities on the road.
But Pierre Bayle, chief SFOR spokesman in Mostar, told Reuters two Croat truck drivers were beaten up by Moslems on the outskirts of the town hours later after nightfall.
